newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: France key player in election for top U.N. post.
newsitem.headline: France key player in election for top U.N. post.

text.p: With Kofi Annan, the Ghanaian head of U.N. peacekeeping, leading in the race for a new U.N. secretary-general, France holds the key on whether he will succeed Boutros Boutros-Ghali in office.

The 15-member Security Council on Tuesday and Wednesday held five rounds of informal voting meant to "discourage" or "encourage" four declared candidates from Africa, which is given preference in fielding nominees.
It will resume unofficial polling on Thursday.
Annan, an American-educated U.N. undersecretary-general, received 11 votes in favour and 4 against, one of them from France, which holds veto power, diplomats said.

He was the only candidate on Wednesday to gain the required nine votes, including those of the United States, Britain, China and Russia, all permanent members with veto rights. But a negative vote from France, when official balloting begins, would doom his candidacy.
No formal vote has been held since Washington vetoed Boutros-Ghali on Nov. 19 while the other 14 council members supported him. His five-year term expires on December 31.

Washington contends Boutros-Ghali, a former Egyptian deputy prime minister, author and French-educated law professor, is too weak in reforming the world body, a position shared by few other countries.
Envoys say the United States and Britain this week voted against the three other African candidates on the list, all from French-speaking nations.

France's favourite candidate is believed to be Amara Essy, the foreign minister of the Ivory Coast and the 1994-95 U.N. General Assembly president, who speaks halting English. He received six yes votes, with four countries opposed, including the United States and Britain. Five states abstained.
French envoys privately say they have no particular grievance against Annan, who does speak French, but prefer other African candidates, such as Essy and Amadou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania.
Ould-Abdallah, a former foreign minister, who was once the U.N. envoy to Burundi, received three votes.
The fourth candidate, Hamid Algabid, a former Niger prime minister and the secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, received two votes.

The next step, diplomats say, is to either convince France to change its mind or find a compromise candidate. President Jacques Chirac has already indicated he would veto Salim A. Salim, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity because he does not speak French.

But envoys say France would be amenable to Lakhdar Brahimi, an Algerian, who last year ran the U.N. operation in Haiti, or Alassane Ouattara of the Ivory Coast, who is a vice president of the International Monetary Fund.

Another potential candidate is Olara Otunnu, the popular Ugandan-born head of the International Peace Academy, a New York-based think tank. Otunnu, now an Ivory Coast citizen, apparently faces opposition from Uganda.
Boutros-Ghali suspended his candidacy Dec. 4 and could reactivate it any time. But he is believed certain to be vetoed again by the United States.
